walkthroughs.body_html:
Coursework — a core area of GCSE English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coursework brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Coursework.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How many witches appear in Macbeth?
What did Romantic poets value in nature?
options: Nature as a source of spiritual insight and emotional truth, accessed through imagination — not picturesque scenery for its own sake.
Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
Genre means whether a book is fiction or non-fiction.
Romantic poets just liked to write about pretty landscapes.

mcqs.q: Why are genre conventions important when interpreting a text?
options: Genre means whether a book is fiction or non-fiction.
Genre is just a label to help bookshops categorise novels.
Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
They set reader expectations the text can fulfil or subvert; analysing how a text uses or breaks conventions reveals its meaning and significance.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
